messages.body_plain:
I will be giving a workshop on March 21 in Kansas City prior to the meetings of the The Association for Education Finance and Policy

Details at the bottom of this message.

Register at: http://aefpweb.org/conferences/inference-workshop#register

I will also be teaching my approaches to Sensitivity/Robustness as part of my course on multiple regression.  This will be April 1 and 3 from 1pm-2:20pm in room 275 Giltner Hall at Michigan State, but you can also join via zoom: https://msu.zoom.us/j/783760435.  Download for 2 minutes and you will be ready.  You can call in at (415) 762-9988 or (646) 568-7788. Meeting ID is 783-760-435

Both are based on materials at: https://msu.edu/~kenfrank/research.htm#causal

There will also be a paper on Konfound coming out in the STATA journal. Details at the bottom of this message.

What would it take to Change your Inference? Quantifying the Discourse about Causal Inferences in the Social Sciences

March 21 Kansas City Missouri, AEFP.  http://aefpweb.org/conferences/inference-workshop#register

Motivation
Statistical inferences are often challenged because of uncontrolled bias. There may be bias due to uncontrolled confounding variables or non-random selection into a sample. We will answer the question about what it would take to change an inference by formalizing the sources of bias and quantifying the discourse about causal inferences in terms of those sources. For example, we will transform challenges such as “But the inference of a treatment effect might not be valid because of pre-existing differences between the treatment groups” to questions such as “How much bias must there have been due to uncontrolled pre-existing differences to make the inference invalid?” “QQQ% of the cases would have to be replaced with cases with no treatment effect to change the inference.”

Approaches
In part I we will use Rubin’s causal model to interpret how much bias there must be to invalidate an inference in terms of replacing observed cases with counterfactual cases or cases from an unsampled population. In part II, we will quantify the robustness of causal inferences in terms of correlations associated with unobserved variables or in unsampled populations. Calculations for bivariate and multivariate analysis will be presented using an app: http://konfound-it.com as well as macros in STATA and R and a spreadsheet for calculating indices [KonFound-it!].

Format
The format will be a mixture of presentation, individual exploration, and group work. Participants may include graduate students and professors, although all must be comfortable with basic regression and multiple regression. Participants should bring their own laptop, or be willing to work with another student who has a laptop. Participants may choose to bring to the course an example of an inference from a published study or their own work, as well as data analyses they are currently conducting.

The workshop will be provided by Ken Frank MSU Foundation Professor of Sociometrics in Measurement and Quantitative Methods at Michigan State University in Counseling, Educational Psychology and Special Education.

Register at: http://aefpweb.org/conferences/inference-workshop#register

KONFOUND: Stata Module to Quantify Robustness of Causal Inferences

Ran Xu1*, Kenneth A. Frank2, Spiro J. Maroulis3, Joshua M. Rosenberg4

1 Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering, Virginia Tech, Falls Church, Virginia, USA

2  Department of Counseling, Educational Psychology and Special Education <http://ed-web3.educ.msu.edu/CEPSE/>, Michigan State University, East Lansing, Michigan, USA

3  School of Public Affairs, Arizona State University, Tempe, Arizona, USA

4  College of Education, Health, and Human Sciences, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Tennessee, USA

* Correspondence to ra...@vt.edu

Abstract. Statistical methods that quantify the discourse about causal inferences in terms of possible sources of biases, also known as “robustness or sensitivity analysis,” are becoming increasingly important to a variety of social-science fields, such as public policy, sociology, and education. A series of recent works by Frank and colleagues on robustness analysis extends earlier methods. We implement these recent developments in STATA. In particular, we provide STATA routines to quantify the % bias necessary to invalidate an inference from a Rubin causal model framework, as well as the robustness of causal inferences in terms of correlations associated with unobserved variables.

messages.subject: Re: Error in R using test_all for merMod Objects
messages.subject_clean: Error in R using test_all for merMod Objects
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jim, and thank you for your message. Thank you too for the reproducible example. Part of why we didn't catch this error before was that we were using the sleepstudy data (built-in to lme4), which only has one predictor variable! Thanks again.
We just pushed an update which I believe fixes the bug. Could you install the development version (i.e., via devtools::install_github("jrosen48/konfound")) and let us know that it worked?
We also added a test--and added an acknowledgement in the news file for the next release (to J Murphy). If you would prefer we don't include your name in the news file, please let us know and we'll remove that.
-Josh

On Mon, Jan 28, 2019 at 1:13 AM Jim Murphy <jpc.m...@gmail.com> wrote:
> I'm trying to work with the konfound R library using mixed effects objects (from lme4). I'm encountering an error when setting test_all=TRUE. (Different errors depending on whether one also includes or omits something for the tested_variable parameter.) The equivalent syntax for the exquivalent lm() models work fine.
>
> The errors are below with a reproducible examples, both those that work and those that don't. Thanks in advance for your help.
>
> library(konfound)
> library(lme4)
> library(mice)   #for example multivariate multilevel data popmis
>
> data(popmis) #example data from mice
>
> #as hlm (1a works; 1b and 1c do not)
> testmod1 <- lmer(teachpop ~ texp + sex + (1| school), data=popmis)
> testkon1a <- konfound(testmod1, texp, to_return = "raw_output")
> Note that the Kenward-Roger approximation is used to estimate degrees of freedom for the predictor(s) of interest.
>
> testkon1b <- konfound(testmod1, texp, test_all=TRUE, to_return = "raw_output")
> Error in if (abs(obs_r) > abs(critical_r)) { :
>   missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed
> In addition: Warning message:
> In data.frame(t = est_eff/std_err, df = df_kr) :
>   row names were found from a short variable and have been discarded
>
> testkon1c <- konfound(testmod1, test_all=TRUE, to_return = "raw_output")
> Error in data.frame(t = est_eff/std_err, df = df_kr) :
>   arguments imply differing number of rows: 4, 0
>
> #as ols (all work)
> testmod2 <- lm(teachpop ~ texp + sex, data=popmis)
> testkon2a <- konfound(testmod2, texp, to_return = "raw_output")
> Note that this output is calculated based on the correlation-based approach used in mkonfound()
>
> testkon2b <- konfound(testmod2, texp, test_all=TRUE, to_return = "raw_output")
> testkon2c <- konfound(testmod2, test_all=TRUE, to_return = "raw_output")
>
